text: Four lessons, four separate pieces of one single skill. This final lesson of the chapter puts every one of them together into a single build process, from a completely blank page all the way to a finished executive dashboard.

Answer the four audience questions first, for your actual real audience. Keep only the metrics that would genuinely change a decision if they moved, and make sure each survivor has a real target to compare against, not just a raw value. Sketch placement by reading order before you build anything at all — headline metric top-left, decreasing in prominence as you move right and down. Choose every visual against the distortion checklist from last lesson, with consistent scale and color throughout the whole page. And fit the entire thing to one screen, with absolutely no scrollbars.

Here's that entire process, already finished and working. One card for the single headline number. Charts that answer compared to what, and broken down how. Nothing more detailed than an executive actually needs at a glance, and nothing left sitting at a Power BI default setting — no three-D effects, no more than a handful of colors repeated consistently, no chart fighting for attention with the one sitting right next to it.

Before calling any executive dashboard finished, run the checklist one more time, tile by tile. Does every single tile trace back to an actual, real audience need? Does every KPI have a genuine target, not just a value? Is the most important number on the page the very first thing the eye lands on? Does every chart avoid last lesson's distortions, with sorting that's deliberate rather than left at the default?

A well-designed dashboard still has to actually reach its audience — published, shared, and kept genuinely up to date. That's exactly where Chapter Nine picks up: Power BI Service and Fabric, workspaces, publishing, and controlling who sees what once your dashboard leaves Power BI Desktop for good.
